analysis.investment_thesis: Firstsource is a mid-sized BPO with decent fundamentals but at INR 16,539 Cr market cap and 24x P/E, it fails the SMILE framework on its most critical filters — it is neither small nor cheap. Revenue CAGR of just 10.6% over 9 years offers no multibagger narrative for a Kedia-style bet.
key_strengths: Revenue accelerated sharply in FY25 to ₹7,980 Cr (+26% YoY), suggesting possible acquisition-led transformation
Promoter holding at 53.66% shows adequate skin-in-the-game; OCF positive all 5 years
Operating income CAGR (13.4%) outpaces revenue CAGR (10.6%), indicating some operating leverage
key_risks: Market cap ₹16,539 Cr is 16x Kedia's ₹1,000 Cr upper limit — no asymmetric upside possible at this size
Debt surged from ₹1,526 Cr to ₹2,369 Cr in one year (D/E 0.54, approaching red-flag zone); cash near zero at ₹13 Cr
FCF declining trend (₹806 Cr in FY21 → ₹477 Cr in FY25) despite revenue growth — capital intensity rising
red_flags: Market cap ₹16,539 Cr — massively outside SMILE sweet spot of <₹1,000 Cr
P/E at 24.1x breaches the 20x red-flag threshold for a BPO with <11% operating margins
Finance costs exploded from ₹155 Cr to ₹184 Cr; borrowings jumped ₹843 Cr in FY25 alone — debt-funded acquisition risk
Net profit CAGR of just 9.6% over 9 years — no earnings acceleration story
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Firstsource is fundamentally not a Kedia stock. The SMILE framework requires small size as its very first filter, and at ₹16,539 Cr this company is a large-cap BPO subsidiary of RPSG Ventures. The information asymmetry edge that creates multibaggers simply does not exist at this scale — institutions own 34% and this stock is well-covered. The 9-year revenue CAGR of 10.6% and net profit CAGR of 9.6% are barely ahead of nominal GDP growth, which is the opposite of what a transformation story looks like.

The one genuinely interesting data point is FY25: revenue jumped 26% to ₹7,980 Cr and operating income hit ₹1,238 Cr — likely driven by a large acquisition (investing CF of -₹744 Cr). However, this came at the cost of a debt binge (borrowings +₹843 Cr, cash collapsed to ₹13 Cr) and a FCF decline to ₹477 Cr. At 24x trailing P/E and 1.81x P/S for a business with sub-12% operating margins, the market is already pricing in recovery. A Kedia investor would need to find this company at ₹500-800 Cr market cap with 20%+ growth to get excited — not at ₹16,500 Cr chasing a BPO roll-up story.
